name: Ivan Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Ivan. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take first calls for a car insurance company, the ones that come in right after a crash. Someone's standing on the hard shoulder shaking, and my job is to get the details down and calm them enough to tell me which way the other car was going. Then I book the tow truck and the hire car. I like that I'm useful at a bad moment; what wears me out is the system freezing while someone's crying down the line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm twenty-seven, I live with Lena, my girlfriend, she's a pharmacy technician. We rent a flat above a bakery, which smells great at six in the morning. I've got about eight months of pay saved and a small shares account my uncle got me started on. I play five-a-side on Thursdays with two guys from the claims floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool like any other. We already have the thing that writes up the call summary for you, and it's handy about half the time. I'd say that at work and probably nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm fine. The summary tool gets a bit better, maybe the hire car booking goes automatic, and I spend more time on the actual person. Honestly that sounds like a better job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd use the summary tool a bit more once the rest of the team says it's stopped making mistakes. I'd keep putting two hundred a month into the shares account and look at the claims handler role, which pays better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. Nothing in it keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said once the team says it's stopped making mistakes. Why wait for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been burned. Last year the summary tool wrote that a customer hit a deer when it was a dog, and I didn't check, and the claim got bounced. Now I let Kemal from five-a-side find the bugs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything else on your mind for the next few years, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, like everyone. And Lena wants a dog, which means moving somewhere with a garden. But we can afford it, it's more about finding the place.

say: I'd say AI is a **tool like any other** and the summary tool helps half the time.
I'd keep my view **at work** and not bother posting online.
think: I'm fine, and automatic **hire car booking** frees time for the person on the line.
The job might actually become **a better job**.
do: Use the **summary tool** more once teammates say the mistakes are fixed.
Keep putting **£200 a month** into my shares account.
Apply for the better-paid **claims handler** role.
feel: Relaxed, with **nothing** about it keeping me awake.
S0.quote: Last year the summary tool wrote that a customer hit a deer when it was a dog, and I didn't check, and the claim got bounced.
fieldNote: Ivan's caution about AI comes from **one bad mistake** rather than any principle.
He lets colleagues **test tools first**, then follows, a steady adopter.
His main life pressure is finding a flat with a **garden** for a dog.

steps.text: Use the call summary tool more once Kemal says it works
Keep putting 200 a month into the shares account
Apply for the claims handler role on the same floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was coming and we should be talking about how it's done, not whether. On the five-a-side group chat I'd be the one saying don't panic, look at the retraining offer first. I'm not a picket-line person, but I'm not a cheerleader for the company either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, first notice of loss is a script. Name, policy number, where, when, which way. A good AI could take that down from a crying person. Probably better than I can at the end of a twelve-hour shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever the company offers on the new system in the first month, before the slots fill. I'd also ask about the motor engineer assessor team, the people who actually go out and look at damaged cars, because that's hands-on. And I'd put a bit more in savings, maybe three hundred instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Not scared yet, but I'd be checking the internal job board every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a good AI might do your job better at the end of a twelve-hour shift. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I like being the calm voice. But if I'm honest, at hour eleven I'm not that calm, I'm just reading the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably hold off on the dog and the garden flat for a year. We'd want to see where my job lands first. Lena's job is safe, people always need prescriptions, so we wouldn't starve.

say: I'd say the question is **how it's done**, not whether it happens.
In the group chat I'd tell people to check the **retraining offer** before panicking.
think: First notice of loss is **basically a script**, which AI could take down well.
At hour eleven of a shift, I'm **not that calm** anyway.
do: Sign up for the **new system training** in the first month.
Ask about the **motor engineer assessor** team that inspects damaged cars.
feel: **Unsettled** but not scared, checking the job board every morning.
S1.quote: First notice of loss is a script. Name, policy number, where, when, which way. A good AI could take that down from a crying person.
fieldNote: Ivan admits AI could do his core task better when he's **tired**.
He'd learn the system early but also scout **hands-on assessor** work as a hedge.
Lena's **secure job** cushions the household, so he delays rather than cancels plans.

steps.text: Join the insurer's training on the new claims system in month one
Ask to shadow the motor engineer assessor team
Put off the dog and garden flat for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when the government has to step in, at least with notice periods and some money for retraining. I'd be careful though, I wouldn't want to sound like a doom merchant at work. Most of the floor would be panicking already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real talk, my job goes in the first wave. A phone line where you take down facts and book a tow truck is exactly what AGI does on day one. Assessing a smashed car still needs hands and eyes for about three years after that, so that's my lifeboat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to get onto the assessor team in the next six months, even at the same pay. I'd stop the shares top-ups and keep cash, because if half the call centres in town close at once, plenty of similar jobs nearby means nothing. I'd also do a short course on vehicle damage, there's one at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly. My stomach drops a bit just saying it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned plenty of jobs nearby. Doesn't that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the other call centres are still hiring. They'd all be buying the same AI at the same time. Plenty of jobs becomes plenty of people chasing none, when every call centre in town buys the same AI at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after the robots come for car assessing, around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-two with some savings and no plan. I'd figure it out then, maybe with Lena's dad, who has a small building firm. But I'd be lying if I said I knew.

say: I'd say government must give **notice periods** and money for retraining.
I'd avoid sounding like a **doom merchant** on a floor already panicking.
think: My job goes in the **first wave**, because it's facts and bookings.
Assessing damaged cars gives me about **three extra years**.
do: Push to join the **assessor team** within six months, even at the same pay.
Stop the shares top-ups and **hold cash** instead.
Take the college's short **vehicle damage** course.
feel: Properly **worried**, with a sinking stomach just saying it.
S2.quote: Plenty of jobs becomes plenty of people chasing none, when every call centre in town buys the same AI at the same time.
fieldNote: Ivan sees that nearby **call centres** would all automate together, so local jobs won't save him.
The **hands-on** assessor role is his lifeboat, but only for about three years.
He has **no plan** past 2031 and says so honestly.

steps.text: Move onto the motor engineer assessor team within six months
Stop shares top-ups and keep savings as cash
Take the college's short course on vehicle damage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if people use it. I'd probably say that at the five-a-side pub afterwards, and Kemal would tell me I'm too optimistic. I'd still say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is about one career move for me. If I get onto the assessor team in year one or two, I've got maybe six years of hands-on work before robots catch up. That's long enough to get really good and save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for assessor training within a year and do the vehicle damage course at night. I'd keep putting money in shares, actually, because if the big companies get rich off AI, I want a slice. Lena and I would still get the dog, just in a cheaper area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's manageable but it's always there, like knowing your contract ends on a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep investing in shares. Isn't that a bet on the thing that takes your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'm fine with that. If I can't beat AI, I might as well own a tiny bit of it. My uncle always said own the factory, not the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the claims floor would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margit, my team leader, honestly. She's brilliant on the phones but she's fifty-three and her whole career is managing call queues. There's no robot-proof version of that.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if people use it well.
I'd keep saying it even when Kemal calls me **too optimistic**.
think: Five years is about **one career move**, and assessing gives six more after that.
That's long enough to **get good** at it and save hard.
do: Apply for **assessor training** within a year and study vehicle damage at night.
Keep investing in **shares** to own a slice of AI's gains.
Get the dog with Lena in a **cheaper area**.
feel: Uneasy, like knowing a **contract end date**.
S3.quote: If I can't beat AI, I might as well own a tiny bit of it. My uncle always said own the factory, not the job.
fieldNote: Ivan treats shares as a **hedge** against the technology that threatens him.
He's still anxious but has a **clear path** with five years.
He worries for **Margit**, his older team leader, more than himself.

steps.text: Apply for motor engineer assessor training within a year
Keep putting money into the shares account each month
Rent a cheaper flat with a garden and get the dog

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time and anyone who doesn't prepare only has themselves to blame. Maybe that's harsh. I'd say it more gently to my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. Ten years gets me to thirty-seven. I could become an assessor, do it for years, maybe even run a small body shop by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the phones a couple more years and go for claims handler first, for the pay. Then assessor training in year three or four. I'd keep saving and investing at the normal rate, and Lena and I would probably buy a place rather than rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit uneasy at the edges, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who don't prepare only have themselves to blame. Would you include yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If I'm still on the first-notice line in 2034, that's on me. Ten years of warning is more than my dad ever got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Varga Electric, my dad's shop, went under when the big chains came to town. He had about six months' warning. So ten years feels generous to me.

say: I'd say **ten years** is loads of time to prepare.
I'd soften it for my mum, admitting the blame line is **a bit harsh**.
think: Ten years gets me to **thirty-seven**, with time to become an assessor.
I might even run a small **body shop** by then.
do: Go for the **claims handler** role first, for the pay.
Start **assessor training** in year three or four.
Buy a place with Lena **instead of renting**.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a little unease at the edges.
S4.quote: If I'm still on the first-notice line in 2034, that's on me. Ten years of warning is more than my dad ever got.
fieldNote: His father's **shop closing** with little warning makes ten years feel generous.
Ivan holds **himself accountable**, a pragmatic centre view.
He plans a **staged** route: pay rise first, then assessor training.

steps.text: Apply for the claims handler role in the next two years
Start motor engineer assessor training in year three or four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My job sits right at the front of the queue. What would help is the insurer being honest early, like telling us a year ahead which teams are going, and paying for assessor training for anyone who wants it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who calms the customer down. The AI can take the facts, but a lot of people ring us just needing someone to say you're okay, you did nothing wrong. A crash call is mostly that.

headlineQuote: The AI can take the facts, but a lot of people ring us just needing someone to say you're okay, you did nothing wrong.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** car insurance agent who takes the first calls after crashes.
He lives with Lena, a pharmacy technician, with **eight months saved** and a small shares account.
He uses AI tools **once proven**, after one bad summary mistake taught him caution.
He moves from calm to **alarmed**, with hands-on **motor assessing** as his route out.
He blames nobody but himself if he wastes **ten years** of warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job is first in the queue.
whatWouldHelp: **Early honesty** from the insurer about which teams go.
Paid **assessor training** for anyone who wants it.
